year fixed refinance 6.65% 15 year fixed refinance 6.03% 10 year fixed refinance 5.98% 5/1 ARM refinance 6.04% Current mortgage refinance news - April 21, 2026 The average rate on a 30-year mortgage fell to 6.34% last week, Bankrate’s weekly survey of lenders showed. That’s down from 6.40% the previous week, but the recent increase in rates — from a 2026 low of 6.09% — had brought refinancing activity to a near-halt. However, the Mortgage Bankers Association reported last week that its Refinance Index was up 15% compared to a year ago. “Borrowers aren’t rushing to act, but they are becoming more aware of the opportunity,” says Kyle Bass, production business manager at Refi.com. “If rates continue to trend in this direction, even gradually, this kind of early reengagement can build into more meaningful refinance activity in the weeks ahead.” Only a minority of homeowners benefit from refinancing now: Most Americans are locked into rates well below 5%, so as long as rates stay above 6%, few people will refinance. And housing economists expect rates to remain above that level as the year progresses. In the past few years, homeowners have turned away from refinancing and toward home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans. However, if you’re hoping for another refinancing boom, be careful what you wish for — a plunge in rates typically occurs only after a recession or other economic shock. Today’s refinance rates Ask the Experts Is now the right time to refinance? How to get the best refinance rate There are many variables that determine your mortgage interest rate, including overarching economic factors like inflation. But your individual factors play the biggest role, such as: Lender Loan type Income Credit score Loan-to-value (LTV) ratio These tips can help increase your odds of getting the best possible rate: Nail down your goals: This will help you decide what term — 30 years, 15 years or something else — is best for you. For example, if your aim is to pay down your loan quickly, a shorter term might make more sense. Shop around: Get rate quotes from at least three mortgage lenders, ideally on the same day so you have an accurate basis for comparison. Here's how to shop for and compare mortgage offers. Compare the interest rate and APR: The interest rate and annual percentage rate (APR) both reflect the cost of the loan. The interest rate is the cost to borrow the funds, while the APR includes the interest rate plus other costs, such as the origination fee and any mortgage points. Consider the lender’s ratings and your experience: Aside from the numbers, evaluate lenders for convenience and responsiveness. Take a look at what other borrowers have had to say about them, too. Should you refinance your mortgage? Whether you should refinance your mortgage right now depends on a few factors: Can you get a significantly lower rate? Refinancing to a lower rate will lower your monthly payment and help you save money over the loan term. Are you shifting from a variable rate to a fixed rate? If you have an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) that’s resetting soon, refinancing to a fixed-rate loan would provide a more predictable payment for your budget going forward. Do you want to change your term? Many people also adjust the length of their mortgage when they refinance. Typically this means shortening the term from 30 years to 15 years to pay off the mortgage faster, or lengthening the term up to 30 years to reduce the monthly payments. Do you want to tap your equity? Many people choose a cash-out refinance to turn their home equity into cash by borrowing against it. This cash can then be used to make home renovations, pay college tuition or cover other major expenses. Can you afford closing costs? Refinancing is essentially taking out a whole new home loan, which comes with a whole new set of closing costs to pay. These can run many thousands of dollars, so make sure your budget can take the hit. Once you know the answers to those questions, review the pros and cons: Pros Checkmark IconYou can lock in a lower rate, which can reduce your monthly payments and total interest paid. Checkmark IconYou can change the length of your loan term and rate type. Checkmark IconIf your home’s value has increased, you might be able to stop paying for private mortgage insurance (PMI). Checkmark IconIf you need money for renovations, a cash-out refi offers relatively cheap capital. It can make your monthly payments more expensive, but home improvements tend to boost your home’s value. Cons Refinance closing costs can equal 2% to 5% of the amount of the mortgage. For example, on a $350,000 loan, expect to pay between $7,000 and $17,500 for closing costs. As such, it can take several years to realize the savings of a mortgage refinance. If you refinance from a 30-year loan to another 30-year loan, you’ll extend your repayment period. How to refinance your mortgage The process of refinancing your mortgage is similar to the process you went through when you applied for your initial one. Here’s an overview of the steps: Check your credit score: Refinances typically require a credit score of at least 620, but a better score will help you secure a better rate and make your refi even more cost-effective. You can check your credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com. Choose a refinance type: Many borrowers opt for a rate-and-term refinance, which changes the interest rate, term or both. (This isn’t the only way to refinance a mortgage, however.) Calculate the break-even timeline: A refi usually comes with upfront costs at closing, just like a home-purchase mortgage. While the closing costs might not be as much, they can still add up to a significant sum. Our refinance break-even calculator can help you figure out when you’ll start realizing savings. Estimate your equity: If you want to refinance to a bigger mortgage and take cash out of your home, it's important to know how much available equity you have. Here's how to calculate your home equity. Compare refinance rates: Explore refinance offers from at least three mortgage lenders, and keep an eye on rates while you comparison-shop. This can help you decide when to lock in a rate. Organize your paperwork: Among the requirements, your lender will want to review tax returns, pay stubs and other proof of income, as well as documentation about any assets or debt. Staying organized can help the process run more smoothly. Apply: Once you know which lenders you're interested in and have your documents ready, complete an application to learn your specific refinance rate and terms. FAQs Jeff Ostrowski covers mortgages and the housing market. Before joining Bankrate in 2020, he spent more than 20 years writing about real estate, business, the economy and politics.
